records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Narcissus tazetta page gives five common names in alphabetical order, in its page-title parenthetical (Bunchflower Daffodil, Cream Narcissus, Paper White Narcissus, Polyanthos Narcissus, Tezetta Daffodils) and in the same order in its Common Name(s) list, and its description text calls the plant Paper White Narcissus. RHS's dedicated profile, Narcissus tazetta (13), gives the common name bunch-flowered daffodil and lists Chinese sacred lily, French daffodil, polyanthus daffodil, polyanthus narcissus and St Joseph's staff as other common names, with no paper-white name. RHS gives the paper-white names to Narcissus papyraceus (paper-white daffodil; other common name paper-white narcissus), whose RHS profile lists Narcissus tazetta subsp. papyraceus among its synonyms. NC State's Quick ID Hints for this species say 'Corona is yellow', while RHS describes Narcissus papyraceus as bearing pure white flowers. Landed as Bunchflower Daffodil, the name both dedicated pages lead with (NC State's Bunchflower Daffodil, RHS's bunch-flowered daffodil). This batch was researched as Paperwhite Narcissus; that one-word spelling appears on neither dedicated page. Distinct from Narcissus pseudonarcissus, landed in this catalog as Daffodil.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Narcissus tazetta page. Pet scope: its Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses (also carried as the tags #problem for cats, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses); the page gives no animal-specific symptoms. Above its Description the page carries the banner 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.', and it has a separate human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' block: Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: 'Vomiting, salvation, diarrhea; large ingestions cause convulsions, low blood pressure, tremors, and cardiac arrhythmias. Bulbs are the most poisonous part'. Poison Toxic Principle: Lycorine and other alkaloids. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. The page has no Poison Part field; the symptoms text names the bulbs as the most poisonous part. Its Plant Type values are Bulb and Herbaceous Perennial, and its description says 'This plant is pest and disease free due to its poisonous alkaloid content.' Sources disagree on skin contact: RHS's species profile, Narcissus tazetta (13), has no toxicity field, but RHS's profile for the nominate subspecies, Narcissus tazetta subsp. tazetta (13), reads under Potentially harmful: 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats, tortoises): Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants'. No source states a preparation that makes any part edible.
unknowns: NC State Plant Toolbox is the only admissible page with care data for Narcissus tazetta that could be read. RHS has a dedicated profile, Narcissus tazetta (13) (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/132835/narcissus-tazetta-(13)/details), but it gives only names and botanical details: the common name bunch-flowered daffodil, other common names, Name Status Correct and Horticultural Group Division 13, with no position, soil, moisture, pH, size or toxicity fields. RHS's profile for the nominate subspecies, Narcissus tazetta subsp. tazetta (13), does carry them (Position Full sun, Partial shade; Moisture Moist but well–drained or Well–drained; pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral; Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres, about 4-20 inches) as well as a Potentially harmful field; it is a narrower taxon, so no care field was taken from it, and its toxicity text is disclosed in toxicity_detail. MoBot Plant Finder returned no results for 'narcissus tazetta' (its Narcissus details page could not be loaded either: the host's certificate chain failed verification from this machine). Clemson is only linked from NC State as a forcing-bulbs article and was not used. No UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for this species was found. scientific_name_accepted rests on NC State's page binomial and on RHS's Name Status Correct.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives Plant Type Bulb and Herbaceous Perennial, USDA zones 7a-10b and Landscape Location Container, Lawn and Walkways, and its planting directions are for in-ground fall planting. Its only indoor mention is a pointer to a Clemson HGIC article 'on forcing bulbs, N. tazetta in particular, for indoor flowers'; forcing bulbs in pebbles or water for a single indoor bloom is not houseplant culture and is not a soil claim. RHS gives a Houseplants type tag only to Narcissus papyraceus, which this record does not draw on.

toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's Problems values Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs (also carried as the tags #problem for cats and #problem for dogs); NC State states no pet-specific symptoms or severity. RHS's profile for the nominate subspecies, Narcissus tazetta subsp. tazetta, agrees: 'Pets (dogs, cats, tortoises): Harmful if eaten; skin irritant.' The Low severity rating comes from NC State's human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block. Skin contact is disputed: NC State's Causes Contact Dermatitis field reads No, while RHS's subspecies profile says 'skin irritant' and 'Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.'; toxicity_detail carries both.

is_edible false is based on NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (vomiting, diarrhea, and in large ingestions convulsions and cardiac arrhythmias, bulbs most poisonous); no source states any part is eaten.

water_regime keep_moist comes from NC State's watering sentence (uniformly moist with good drainage during the growing season, drought tolerated while dormant). Counterpoint: the same description says 'medium moisture' soils, 'tolerates heat, but not extremely wet conditions' and 'Bulb rot can occur in wet soils', so soil_drainage is moderate, not moisture_retentive.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours) and Partial Shade (2-6 hours), and the description says full sun to part shade; Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the only hour figures are the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose.

Soil pH left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0); Acid is open-ended so no floor is set, and RHS's species profile has no pH field to check the closed top of the Neutral band against, so no ceiling is set from it (RHS's nominate-subspecies profile reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which would not allow one either).

Size: this NC State page has no structured Dimensions block. Its prose says it typically grows to 18 inches tall but has been known to reach 30 inches, so only the maximum height (30 in) is filled and the minimum is left null. No spread is stated: 'Available Space To Plant: Less than 12 inches' and the 4 to 10 inch bulb spacing are planting guidance, not mature spread.
attracts_pollinators left null: this NC State page carries no Attracts field and no Landscape Theme field, and no pollinator statement.

Left null with no source support: temperatures, humidity, indoor foot-candle light, fertilizer interval/strength/months (NC State only says bone meal or super phosphate in the planting hole), chill damage onset (NC State's hardiness zones 7a-10b are not a damage onset), watering day estimates and dry-down target (in-ground bulb).

common_name researched as 'Paperwhite Narcissus' (the batch brief's name); landed as 'Bunchflower Daffodil', the first entry of NC State's alphabetized list and title parenthetical and RHS's lead (bunch-flowered daffodil). NC State's description prose opens with 'Paper White Narcissus', which the landing brief also admits as a lead, but RHS gives the paper-white names to Narcissus papyraceus, a species RHS holds separately (Name Status Correct, with Narcissus tazetta subsp. papyraceus as its synonym), and no admissible page renders the one-word 'Paperwhite'. NC State has no separate Narcissus papyraceus page (its /plants/narcissus-papyraceus/ address returns 404), so within NC State the paper-white name belongs to this species; switching the landed name back to Paper White Narcissus would be a one-line change.

records.name_note: Of the admissible sources' dedicated pages for this exact name, the two that could be read, NC State's and RHS's, differ on the lead common name. NC State's Common Name(s) list and its page-title parenthetical are alphabetized and begin with Cabbage Palm (then Cabbage Tree, Cornish Palm, Giant Dracaena, New Zealand Cabbage Tree, Torbay Palm, Torquay Palm). RHS's page title, 'Cordyline australis | cabbage palm', gives cabbage palm as its common name, and RHS lists 'cabbage tree' under Other common names. NC State's own description prose calls the plant Cabbage Tree. Cabbage Tree was chosen because it is the name NC State's description prose opens with, because Cabbage Palm is also the title name of a different species, Sabal palmetto (UF/IFAS EDIS: 'Sabal or Cabbage Palm'), and because both pages read carry Cabbage Tree. The plant was formerly Dracaena australis (NC State 'Previously known as'; RHS lists it under Synonyms).
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox page for Cordyline australis. The Problems field carries three tags: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. The page's tag list reads: #problem for horses, #problem for dogs, #problem for cats, #tropical feel, #flowering tree, #small tree, #evergreen, #fragrant flowers, #container plant, #taproot. The page banner reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' and names no scope; the rating itself, Poison Severity: Low, sits in the block headed 'Poisonous to Humans', so it is a human-scoped rating, separate from the Problem-for-Cats/Dogs/Horses tags. Poison Symptoms: 'Poisonous to dogs and cats. Can cause vomiting (occasionally with blood), hypersalivation, dilated pupils (cats).' Dilated pupils is the only symptom the page scopes to cats; the page does not scope the others further. Poison Toxic Principle: Saponins. Poison Part: Fruits, Leaves (the full list, two parts). The page's Problems prose also says 'The plant is toxic for dogs and cats.' Horses appear only as a Problem-for-Horses tag; the page gives no horse-specific symptoms. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No, and the page states no handling warning. EDIBILITY IS SEPARATE AND CONFLICTS WITH THE POISON-PART LIST: NC State's Edibility field says 'The stems and fleshy rhizomes of the tree are high in sugar and used as sweetener. The leaves are eaten raw.' No preparation times or conditions are given, and the page does not reconcile raw leaf eating with Leaves being a listed poison part; the edibility statement is not a safe-to-eat statement. RHS's page for this species carries no toxicity statement, so there is no disagreement between admissible sources on scope (fruit-only versus unrestricted).
unknowns: MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org, taxonid=282400) could not be read: the fetch failed with a certificate-verification error, so nothing is cited from it. The auditor, reading it in a browser, reports a dedicated page for this exact name whose Common Name field reads 'cabbage tree', the landed name; its other statements are unconfirmed here.

No dedicated page for Cordyline australis was found on the other admissible hosts (UF/IFAS EDIS and Ask IFAS, Clemson HGIC, Penn State, UMD, UGA); the only EDIS hit was the Sabal palmetto page, used solely for the name disambiguation in name_note.

is_edible is null, not true (landing decision under the catalog's edibility rule). NC State's Edibility field says 'The stems and fleshy rhizomes of the tree are high in sugar and used as sweetener. The leaves are eaten raw.', with no preparation, time or condition, while the same page's Poisonous to Humans block lists Poison Part Fruits and Leaves with the Poison Symptoms 'Poisonous to dogs and cats. Can cause vomiting (occasionally with blood), hypersalivation, dilated pupils (cats).', and its description says 'The plant is toxic for dogs and cats.' The page does not reconcile raw leaf eating with Leaves being a listed poison part. A sweetener and raw-leaf use stated without context for an ornamental tree that its own page lists as poisonous is a marginal food use, and the app shows is_edible true as 'grown to eat' with no condition, so the field is left null and both statements are carried in toxicity_detail.
Horse toxicity is only the NC State 'Problem for Horses' tag; no horse symptoms are given.

Mature size: this record is framed as a houseplant (NC State: 'grown indoors year-round as a houseplant'), so its height is NC State's container figure: 'It can also be grown as an ornamental in a container and, in that environment, will slowly develop a cane-like trunk or trunks and reach a height of 15 feet.' (180 in, the maximum; no container minimum is given, so mature_height_in_min is null). The outdoor statures are not used for height: NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 6 ft. 0 in. - 30 ft. 0 in. (72-360 in), its description says 'The plant can reach a height of 30 to 60 feet in its native habitat at maturity.', and RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres (157-315 in). The spread is NC State's Dimensions Width 3 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in. (36-72 in), the page's only width figure; RHS gives a larger Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98-157 in), with Time to Maturity 20-50 years. MoBot (reported by the auditor from a browser read; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited) gives Height 6.00 to 15.00 feet and Spread 3.00 to 6.00 feet.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so both ends are open.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State's container-specific, summer-specific sentence; it also says to reduce moisture indoors in winter. NC State's outdoor soil description is moist but well-drained, its Drainage tags span Occasionally Dry and Occasionally Wet, and the prose says the plant tolerates wet boggy to dry soils; RHS gives Moisture 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' and Drought Resistance 'Yes'. Drought tolerance is not read as a watering instruction. No numeric day intervals are stated by either source, so water day estimates, dry-down target and check depth are null.

soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's Drainage tags are Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry and Occasionally Wet, and RHS says moist but well-drained or well-drained. Not fast, because NC State states tolerance of wet boggy conditions.
soil_base garden_bed reflects NC State's soil description for plants grown outdoors; the sources give no potting-mix recommendation for container culture.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State Light tags are Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours of direct sun) and its prose says full sun to part shade; RHS Position lists Full sun, Partial shade. NC State's 'Partial Shade' tag was mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are in NC State's generic light-category legend.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State gives USDA zones 9a-11b and RHS gives hardiness H3, which are hardiness ratings and not a damage-onset temperature. Day and night temperature ranges, humidity, indoor light (foot-candles), fertilizer interval, strength and months are not stated by the sources read, so those fields are null.
RHS Cultivation text ('Grow in well-drained soil in a sheltered position in full sun or partial shade') was not used for any field because it may be shared with sibling Cordyline pages.
NC State describes a taproot and a need for a large, deep container; flowering is rare in containers. These do not fit a schema field.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Poisonous to Humans block; the Poison Severity rating of Low sits under that human-scoped heading, and the page header says "low severity poison characteristics"): "Ingestion causes burning of the mouth, abdominal pain, vomiting, depression, anorexia, hypersalivation, wobbly gait, and bloody diarrhea. Skin redness, burning sensation, and blisters following contact with cell sap." Toxic principle: "Protoanemonin, released from the glycoside ranunculin." Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems. Separate NC State Problems tags, distinct from the human Poison block: Contact Dermatitis, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses (the page tag list also carries #problem for cats, #problem for horses, #problem for dogs, #contact dermatitis). NC State Plant Type values: Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Sap handling warning (separate from ingestion): the skin redness, burning and blisters follow contact with cell sap. RHS (Potentially harmful row, in full): "Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin irritant - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants"; its Pets line names no animal. The RHS and NC State sources agree on harm from eating and skin contact; neither describes any edible use.
unknowns: MoBot carries a dedicated page for this exact taxon (plantfinder.mobot.org PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286205; Common Name: Persian buttercup; Height and Spread 1.00 to 2.00 feet; Sun: Full sun; Water: Medium), consistent with the values landed here (reported by the auditor from a browser read; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited), but plantfinder.mobot.org could not be fetched by non-browser clients from this sandbox, so nothing is cited from it. Other admissible hosts (Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD, UGA) were not found to carry a dedicated page for this exact name and were not used.

NC State's care paragraph is explicitly written about Ranunculus hybrids ('Ranunculus hybrids prefer...'), since most garden plants are cultivars and hybrids. soil_base, chill_damage_f and soil_drainage rest on that hybrid-framed paragraph plus structured fields; chill_damage_f 28 F is NC State's 'incurring injury at temperatures below 28 degrees F' for semi-hardy plants in North Carolina and may not describe the wild species. USDA zones 8a-10b are a hardiness rating, not a damage onset.

soil_drainage is moderate because NC State's structured Soil Drainage pair is Good Drainage + Moist and RHS says Well-drained. NC State's prose says 'excellent drainage' and warns that 'Root rot can occur in wet, poorly drained soils', and no admissible source grants wet tolerance; fast is therefore also defensible, but no source describes the plant as dry-tolerant, so moderate was kept.

water_regime left null: NC State says 'They do best in medium moisture' (mid-scale, not keep_moist) and tags Soil Drainage Moist, but no source gives a watering statement. RHS says only Moisture: Well-drained. RHS says the plant 'Requires a dry, dormant period in summer' and NC State says the plants 'will go dormant in summer'; that is a seasonal rest, not a cadence; no day counts derived.

Size conflict: NC State's species-page Dimensions block gives Height 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in and Width 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in (12-24 in), used here. RHS gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in). The two overlap but differ; NC State's anchor was chosen per the task's size rule, and the NC State dimensions may reflect garden hybrids.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only: NC State Light 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and RHS Position 'Full sun'. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the 6-hour figure there is the site-wide light-category legend text, not species prose.
soil_ph_min/max left null: RHS pH field reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral (no bound); NC State gives no pH.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives Plant Type Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous, USDA zones 8a-10b and Landscape Location Container and Walkways. Its container mentions are not houseplant culture: 'Although they are perennial, these plants are often grown as annuals or grown in containers as florist’s plants.', and tubers 'can be started indoors and planted outside in spring'. RHS's Cultivation line reads 'Requires a dry, dormant period in summer; grows best in containers with a mix of equal parts loam, leaf mould and grit under unheated glass with good light and ventilation'. No admissible page describes growing it as a houseplant.
is_edible false rests on RHS 'Harmful if eaten' and NC State's ingestion symptoms (burning of the mouth, etc.); no source describes any edible use.

Humidity, light in foot-candles, indoor temperature ranges, fertilizing, and cool_rest_note: no admissible source states them, left null. NC State advises storing dug tubers cool and dry but gives no temperature.

toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's Problems values Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs (Problem for Horses is a separate animal); NC State's Poison Severity Low is human-scoped. records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block is human-scoped (heading 'Poisonous to Humans'): Poison Severity Medium, and the page says 'This plant has medium severity poison characteristics.' Poison Toxic Principle: Protoanemonin. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Symptoms (verbatim): 'Toxic if eaten in large quantities and causes severe pain in the mouth. Poisonous by ingestion and dermatitis. All parts of the plant are poisonous. Symptoms: Inflammation and blistering upon contact with fresh sap; irritation of mouth, vomiting and diarrhea following ingestion.' Poison Part (full list as rendered): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Problems tags: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Children. Plant Type tags: Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. The page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag and names no cat or dog; no cat/dog claim is made. Only NC State (one admissible source) addresses toxicity; RHS and the other fetched pages were checked and give no scope disagreement.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's toxicity data is human-scoped and the page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tag; no admissible source names cats or dogs for this species.

Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated Plant Finder page for this species (https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286104, which redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org) is live. This machine's default fetchers reject it because its server omits its intermediate TLS certificate, so nothing is cited from it. Read by the auditor with that certificate supplied, it is consistent with the record. 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' covers both landed sun values. 'Height: 0.75 to 1.50 feet' and 'Spread: 0.50 to 0.75 feet' are 9-18 in and 6-9 in, in line with NC State. Its Culture text calls for 'rich, sandy, medium moisture, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade', which fits moderate drainage. 'Water: Medium' is a mid-scale field that sets no water_regime. Its Common Name field reads 'windflower', a name shared with Anemone blanda and the genus, and its Noteworthy Characteristics adds 'poppy anemone'. It carries no toxicity or edibility statement.

water_regime left null: NC State has no watering statement (its 'Moist' tag is a soil adjective paired with Good Drainage); RHS says only to keep the plant dry while dormant in summer, which is a cultivation note not framed as a watering regime. Water-interval fields and dormant-period estimates left null accordingly.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's bare Good Drainage + Moist pair; NC State's 'Root rot can occur in too wet soils' is a warning against wet soil and does not make drainage fast. RHS's Moisture field says only 'Well-drained', which is ambiguous alone.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), whose outer bands are open-ended, and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured fields give Full sun and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' (mapped to part_shade); its prose says 'full sun to light shade'. RHS lists Position Full sun only, consistent with full_sun. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the only hour figures are NC State's site-wide light legend.

Size: NC State's species-page Dimensions block (Height: 0 ft. 10 in. - 1 ft. 6 in.; Width: 0 ft. 6 in. - 0 ft. 9 in.) is the anchor, giving 10-18 in tall and 6-9 in wide, and its description agrees ('The plant will grow up to 1.5 feet tall and spread 6 to 9 inches wide in full sun to light shade.'). RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread both as the coarse band 0.1-0.5 metres (about 3.9-19.7 in), which contains NC State's figures rather than contradicting them.

chill_damage_f left null: RHS H5 hardiness rating and NC State zones 7a-10b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. Temperature, humidity, light-fc, fertilizer fields have no admissible support and are null.

NC State's page for it is titled 'Dutch Iris - Iris x hollandica', and its Iris x hollandica binomial page lists a single common name, Dutch Iris; RHS's dedicated profile gives the common name Dutch iris; UGA's CAES Field Report feature calls the plant the Dutch iris. records.name_note: Two admissible sources have a dedicated page for this hybrid and they lead with different names. NC State's page title parenthetical begins with Calamansi (its alphabetized Common Name(s) list also begins Calamansi, then Calamondin, Calamondin Orange, Philippine lemon, Philippine Lime), while RHS's page title ends in calamondin and its Other common names line reads calamondin orange, Panama orange, Philippine lime. NC State's own description prose calls the plant Calamondin, so Calamondin is used as the common name. The two parent-species pages were not used. NC State says the plant is thought to be a cross between mandarin orange and a kumquat, so the × hybrid name is kept. RHS lists ×Citrofortunella microcarpa, ×Citrofortunella mitis and Citrus × mitis as synonyms. RHS's page title carries a trailing "(F)", which is not part of the name.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source names this hybrid as toxic or safe for cats or dogs. NC State's page for Citrus x microcarpa carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags, so toxic_to_pets is left null. RHS's Botanical Details on its calamondin page has a Potentially harmful field reading: "Fruit harmful to skin with sunlight/skin allergen (lemon and lime-bearing Citrus only). Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". The page's own parenthetical limits that wording to lemon- and lime-bearing Citrus, and the page does not say whether it applies to this hybrid, so it is reported as given and not as a finding for this plant. Edibility, as the sources state it: NC State: "The fruit is edible and adds a tangy flavor to drinks and foods, such as noodles", and "It is used in drinks and as a flavoring for foods"; the fruit "has a thin, fragrant peel and an acidic pulp". RHS: "Although the fruit is edible and the peel sweet, the pulp is very sour and acidic". No source gives preparation times or a poison-part list for this plant.
unknowns: Hardiness disagreement, recorded and not resolved: NC State's own description says "Sources vary as to what the growing zones are. records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Passiflora caerulea page. Its Landscape "Problems" tags are: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. These tags are separate from the "Poisonous to Humans" block, which is human-scoped: Poison Severity Medium (the page also says "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics."); Poison Symptoms "Severe nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, and episodes of irregular heartbeat."; Poison Toxic Principle cyanogenic glycosides; Causes Contact Dermatitis No; Poison Part Leaves, Stems. Plant Type on the same page: Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Vine. No handling warning is stated. Edibility, stated conditionally by the same page: Edibility field "Plant parts used as a stress-relieving tea. The fruit, while edible, tastes bland." and Fruit Value To Gardener lists Edible and Showy. The tea remark does not override the page's own leaf-and-stem toxicity, and the page gives no preparation instructions, times or conditions for the tea. RHS (its own page for this species) says "Fruits are edible but not particularly tasty" and shows no toxicity statement; it does not address cats or dogs. The two sources do not conflict on fruit edibility, but only NC State addresses toxicity, and its poison parts are leaves and stems, not fruit.
unknowns: is_edible is null, not true (landing decision under the catalog's edibility rule). NC State's Edibility field reads 'Plant parts used as a stress-relieving tea. The fruit, while edible, tastes bland.', its Fruit Value To Gardener field lists Edible and Showy, and RHS says 'Fruits are edible but not particularly tasty'. Neither page says the fruit is grown or used for food. NC State's human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block gives Poison Part Leaves and Stems, Poison Severity Medium, Poison Toxic Principle cyanogenic glycosides and Poison Symptoms 'Severe nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, and episodes of irregular heartbeat.'; its separate Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses without naming a plant part. The tea remark names no part and gives no preparation instructions. A bland-but-edible fruit on a plant with poisonous leaves and stems is a marginal food use, and the app shows is_edible true as 'grown to eat' with no condition, so the field is left null and the statements are carried in toxicity_detail.
